strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation (scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length input) that clearly identifies a gap between single-image camera-control methods and short-window video-to-future-video methods.

The dual spatio-temporal conditioning design is architecturally elegant: it repurposes the existing image-conditioning channel of a pretrained I2V DiT (CogVideoX) to accept both temporal and spatial (projected static point cloud) latents, preserving pretrained priors with minimal fine-tuning (only 4K iterations).

The three-stage dynamic masking pipeline (optical-flow thresholding + SAM2 propagation + CoTracker3 backward tracking) is a sensible and reasonably thorough engineering solution to the static/dynamic separation problem, and the ablation (Table 4) convincingly shows its necessity (removing it hurts PSNR/MEt3R).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning camera controllability (mRotErr/mTransErr/mCamMC), generation quality (FVD, VBench++), and spatial/geometric consistency (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/MEt3R), with consistent improvements over multiple competitive baselines (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D, DFoT).

Notable and large improvement in geometric consistency (MEt3R) over the most directly comparable baseline (DFoT), supporting the core claim that the proposed static 3D memory better preserves scene structure over long horizons.
Reasonable ablation on the number of spatially adjacent views n, showing the method is not overly sensitive to this hyperparameter.
weaknesses: The camera-control/quality baselines in Tables 2-3 (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D) are only given a single image or camera trajectory, while the proposed method also receives the last 9 frames plus a full video for 3D memory construction; this asymmetry makes the comparison less fair and does not isolate the contribution of the proposed spatial-memory component versus simply having more temporal context.

Only one baseline (DFoT) is used for the core scene-consistency claim (Table 1), which is the paper's central contribution; a single-baseline comparison weakens confidence in the generality of the improvement, especially since closely related geometry-grounded methods (Gen3C, TrajectoryCrafter) discussed in related work are not quantitatively compared.

No reported computational cost/latency for the offline 3D scene memory construction pipeline (MegaSAM + optical flow + SAM2 + CoTracker3), despite the paper's repeated claims of computational efficiency; this preprocessing could be substantial for long videos and undermines the 'without sacrificing computational efficiency' claim if unaddressed.

No discussion of scalability/memory cost of the aggregated point cloud itself as input video length grows arbitrarily large — the paper claims to handle 'arbitrary-length' video but doesn't analyze point-cloud storage/rendering cost at scale.

Lack of explicit failure-case analysis or limitations section: no discussion of when the dynamic-masking/SLAM pipeline might fail (fast/complex motion, textureless regions, heavy occlusion, non-rigid scenes) and how errors propagate into the spatial conditioning.
No ablation on the pixel-level motion threshold τ or sensitivity of dynamic masking hyperparameters, despite this being a critical component of the pipeline.
No user study or perceptual evaluation despite strong claims about visual/generation quality improvements; reliance solely on automated metrics (FVD, VBench++) leaves room for metric-gaming concerns.

Training data is limited to RealEstate10K (static) and OpenVid-1M (dynamic); potential domain gap to more diverse or in-the-wild dynamic scenes (e.g., outdoor, crowded, fast-motion) is not discussed or tested.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored problem: combining long-range scene consistency with precise camera control from arbitrary-length video context, rather than single-image or short-clip conditioning.

The dual spatio-temporal conditioning idea (temporal frames for motion continuity + projected static point cloud for spatial consistency) is a reasonable and intuitively motivated design that reuses a pretrained video diffusion backbone (CogVideoX) with minimal architectural changes, which is appealing for practicality.

The dynamic masking pipeline (optical flow thresholding + backward CoTracker3 tracking + SAM2 propagation) is a sensible multi-stage solution to the specific problem of separating static vs. dynamic 3D structure in casual dynamic video, and the qualitative ghosting-artifact comparisons (Fig. 4) support its necessity.

Quantitative results show consistent improvements over DFoT on spatial/geometric consistency metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/MEt3R) and over camera-control/video-quality baselines (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D) on camera accuracy and VBench++/FVD metrics.
Ablations on the number of spatially adjacent views n and on the necessity of dynamic masking are included and support core design choices.
weaknesses: The pipeline is a heavy orchestration of many existing off-the-shelf components (MegaSAM/dynamic SLAM, RAFT/SEA-RAFT optical flow, SAM2, CoTracker3), each pretrained and non-trivial to run; the core technical novelty is mainly in how these are combined rather than a new underlying method, which limits the conceptual contribution relative to the engineering complexity.

No reporting or analysis of computational cost/runtime of the full preprocessing pipeline (SLAM + flow + tracking + segmentation) per input video, despite the paper's repeated claims of 'computational efficiency'; this is a significant omission given the stated goal of handling arbitrary-length videos.

Unclear scalability of the static point cloud memory for truly 'arbitrary-length' videos — memory/size growth of the aggregated point cloud, retrieval cost for top-n spatially adjacent frames, and robustness of the dynamic SLAM/masking pipeline on longer or more complex real-world sequences are not discussed or stress-tested (training videos are only L>100, and evaluation sequences appear short, e.g., T=60).

Ablations are narrow: only n and the presence/absence of dynamic masking are varied; there is no ablation on the temporal window size w, on using naive frame retrieval instead of 3D projection, on alternative SLAM/mask backbones, or on robustness to SLAM/mask failure cases (e.g., fast motion, occlusion-heavy scenes, pose estimation drift in long sequences).

No discussion of failure cases or limitations (e.g., what happens when dynamic SLAM pose estimation is inaccurate over long/casual videos, or when masking fails to capture objects that become dynamic only briefly) — important given the pipeline's reliance on cascaded, error-prone components.

The claim that 'precise camera control' emerges 'without any other explicit camera conditioning' is somewhat misleading, since the camera trajectory is used explicitly to render the projected point-cloud views that condition the model — this is implicit rather than absent camera conditioning, and the phrasing overstates the novelty of this aspect.

Baseline comparisons for scene-consistency (Table 1) are limited to a single competitor (DFoT); no comparison against simpler ablated versions of the proposed method (e.g., naive frame retrieval without masking, or retrieval without 3D projection) is given as a baseline to isolate the benefit of 3D-based warping versus simpler spatial retrieval.

Evaluation is restricted to 1,000 clips from two datasets with revisit-trajectory protocols; no user study or broader out-of-distribution evaluation (e.g., different camera motion styles, more complex multi-person dynamic scenes) is provided to assess generalization.

Training recipe (4K iterations, 48 GPU-hours) and resulting generalization are not stress-tested against longer unseen trajectories beyond the training distribution, raising questions about how well the model generalizes to significantly longer context/camera trajectories than seen in training.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: generating scene-consistent, camera-controllable video continuations from arbitrary-length input, going beyond the short-clip conditioning limitations of prior camera-controllable and video-to-future-video methods.

The core idea of dual spatio-temporal conditioning (temporally adjacent frames for motion continuity + spatially adjacent static-only content for scene consistency) is a clean and intuitive reformulation that cleverly sidesteps the quadratic cost of attending to all input frames.

The 3D scene memory construction via dynamic SLAM plus a carefully designed three-stage dynamic masking pipeline (pixel-level flow thresholding, backward tracking with CoTracker3, propagation with SAM2) is a thoughtful and non-trivial engineering contribution that directly addresses the key failure mode of naive point cloud aggregation (ghosting from dynamic objects).

The approach is built on top of a pretrained video diffusion backbone (CogVideoX-I2V-5B) with minimal architectural changes, preserving pretrained priors while enabling a new conditioning mechanism, which is an efficient and practical design choice.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive, covering spatial/geometric consistency (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/MEt3R), camera controllability (rotation/translation/extrinsic error), and video quality (FVD, VBench++), across both static (RealEstate10K) and dynamic (DynPose-100K) datasets, with consistent improvements over strong and relevant baselines (DFoT, CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D).

Ablation studies validate the necessity of the dynamic masking component and provide reasonable justification for the choice of n (number of spatially adjacent frames), showing the design choices are not arbitrary.
Qualitative results (Fig. 6, 7) are illustrative and support the quantitative claims, particularly on revisited-viewpoint scenarios where competing methods visibly fail to maintain scene structure.
weaknesses: Reliance on an external dynamic SLAM pipeline (MegaSAM) plus a multi-stage masking pipeline (optical flow, SAM2, CoTracker3) introduces significant preprocessing complexity and potential failure points (e.g., inaccurate camera pose estimation in highly dynamic or textureless scenes) that are not thoroughly stress-tested or discussed as limitations.

The evaluation protocol for spatial/geometric consistency relies on camera trajectories that revisit input viewpoints, which is somewhat self-serving to the proposed method's design; broader or more adversarial camera trajectories (e.g., large excursions into unobserved regions) are not deeply analyzed.

No explicit runtime/latency comparison or discussion of the computational overhead introduced by SLAM processing, point cloud projection, and the three-stage masking pipeline relative to baseline methods, despite efficiency being claimed as a key motivation.

Ablation on n is somewhat limited (only tested up to n=L with marginal differences, and no ablation on temporal window size w or on the choice of dynamic masking components individually, e.g., effect of CoTracker3 backward tracking stage alone vs. optical flow alone).

Only one base video diffusion backbone (CogVideoX-I2V-5B) is used; it is unclear how well the dual conditioning mechanism generalizes to other architectures or larger-scale backbones, limiting claims of general applicability.

The paper does not discuss failure cases or limitations of the proposed method itself (e.g., when dynamic masking fails, when static geometry is sparse/occluded, or performance on highly cluttered dynamic scenes), which would strengthen the paper's completeness and honesty about scope.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: preserving scene consistency (not just temporal continuity) while enabling precise camera control from arbitrary-length input videos, going beyond the single-image or short-clip conditioning of prior camera-controllable video generators.

The dual spatio-temporal conditioning design (temporal window for motion continuity + spatially retrieved projected views from a static-only 3D scene memory) is a clean and technically sound reformulation of the adjacency concept in video conditioning, and is well justified via clear comparisons to existing paradigms (Eq. 1-4, Fig. 2).

The three-stage dynamic masking pipeline (optical-flow thresholding, SAM2 object propagation, CoTracker3 backward tracking/aggregation) is a sensible and non-trivial engineering solution to the ghosting artifact problem when aggregating multi-frame point clouds, and its necessity is validated by a dedicated ablation (Tab. 6).

Extensive empirical validation: comparisons against multiple relevant baselines (DFoT, CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D) across camera controllability, video quality (FVD, VBench++), spatial consistency (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), and geometric consistency (MEt3R), on two datasets (RealEstate10K, DynPose-100K), plus long-video generalization on DAVIS.

Thorough ablations covering the number of spatial views n, temporal window size w, necessity of dynamic masking (with per-stage breakdown), and swapping the SLAM backbone (MegaSAM vs DepthAnything v3), along with an inference-time analysis showing the overhead can be substantially reduced.

The method requires no architectural changes to the underlying video diffusion backbone (reuses the image-conditioning channel), which is a practically appealing design choice and aids reproducibility; code is promised to be released.
Qualitative results (Fig. 6, 7, 9-12) convincingly show failure modes of baselines (scene drift, loss of static detail, hallucinated content) that the proposed method avoids.
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead from the SLAM/dynamic-masking preprocessing pipeline (originally ~4 minutes per clip, ~9 minutes total inference vs ~1-2 minutes for baselines); although mitigated with DepthAnything v3, the method remains considerably more complex and resource-intensive than single-image conditioned baselines, and the modularity claim needs more validation across additional SLAM/depth backbones.

The evaluation is limited to a single video diffusion backbone (CogVideoX-I2V-5B); no experiments demonstrate the framework's generality across different pretrained video generators despite the paper's claim that the design is broadly applicable.

No quantitative comparison to the closely related concurrent work SPMem is provided (only qualitative/conceptual discussion), which weakens the positioning of the contribution relative to the most similar prior approach.

No human/perceptual evaluation is included despite the central claims being about subjective scene consistency and visual quality; reliance solely on automated metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD/VBench++/MEt3R) may not fully capture perceptual realism or motion plausibility.

The pipeline's correctness depends on cascading external modules (SEA-RAFT, SAM2, CoTracker3, MegaSAM); failure modes of this multi-stage masking process (e.g., partially occluded or slow-moving dynamic objects, crowded scenes) are not deeply analyzed beyond a brief mention in the limitations section.

Long-horizon (iterative autoregressive) generation still suffers from unresolved temporal drift/error accumulation, as acknowledged by the authors, somewhat limiting the practical significance of the 'arbitrary-length' framing.

Camera-controllable baselines used for comparison are single-image conditioned by design, which may make some comparisons in Table 2/3 less apples-to-apples given the very different amount of context information available to each method.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap: existing camera-controllable video generation methods only condition on a single frame or short clip, failing to preserve long-range scene context, and the proposed dual temporal/spatial conditioning is a reasonable, well-motivated solution.

The dynamic masking pipeline (optical flow thresholding + backward tracking with CoTracker3 + SAM2 propagation) is a thoughtful engineering solution to the practical problem of ghosting artifacts from naively aggregating dynamic points into a static 3D map, and the ablation (Table 6) shows each stage matters.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided for several design choices (temporal window size w, number of spatially-adjacent frames n, choice of SLAM backbone, use of dynamic masking), which helps substantiate some design decisions.

Quantitative improvements over the closest related baseline (DFoT) and several camera-controllable baselines are consistently positive across the reported metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/MEt3R, camera control errors, FVD/VBench++), and qualitative figures illustrate the claimed benefits (scene memory retention, camera fidelity).
The method is largely modular/plug-and-play (SLAM and dynamic-mask components can be swapped, e.g., MegaSAM vs. DepthAnything v3), which is a practical property explicitly demonstrated.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily combinatorial: the core contribution assembles existing off-the-shelf components (dynamic SLAM/MegaSAM, SEA-RAFT optical flow, CoTracker3, SAM2, CogVideoX-I2V backbone) into a pipeline rather than proposing a fundamentally new architecture or learning objective; the conceptual idea of projecting a static point cloud as a conditioning signal is also closely related to prior geometry-grounded video generation work (Gen3C, CameraCtrl2, StarGen, and especially the concurrent SPMem, which is only discussed qualitatively in the appendix rather than benchmarked quantitatively).

The main quantitative comparison for the central claim (scene-consistent long-horizon generation) is against a single baseline, DFoT (Table 1), which is acknowledged to have fundamentally different memory constraints; this is a fairly narrow empirical basis for the central claim of 'significantly outperforming existing methods in scene consistency.'

Several baselines used for camera-controllability and video-quality comparisons (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D) were not designed for the scene-consistent/long-context setting at all (they are single-frame conditioned), making the comparison somewhat unfair/expected to favor the proposed method rather than isolating the actual algorithmic contribution.

The pipeline carries substantial preprocessing cost (MegaSAM-based SLAM + dynamic masking taking ~4 minutes, totaling ~9 minutes per chunk, even ~5 minutes with the lighter DepthAnything v3 variant), which is a nontrivial practical overhead not fully contextualized against simpler baselines beyond raw runtime numbers; scalability to longer inputs/online or interactive settings is unclear.

Evaluation relies on only two datasets (DynPose-100K, RealEstate10K) for the primary tables and DAVIS only for the long-video extension; there is no user study for perceptual quality/consistency, which is common in video generation papers to support subjective claims (e.g., 'maintains scene elements... throughout generation').

The paper builds on and fine-tunes a single specific backbone (CogVideoX-I2V-5B); it is unclear how well the dual spatio-temporal conditioning generalizes to other video diffusion backbones or larger/newer models, limiting claims of general applicability.

The long-video (iterative autoregressive) extension in the appendix shows the method still suffers from the well-known temporal drift/error-accumulation problem, which is acknowledged as unresolved; given that long-horizon consistency is a central motivation of the paper, this limits the significance of the contribution for the headline use case.

Some qualitative comparisons (Figs. 6, 7) are selectively chosen scenes that highlight failure cases of baselines (e.g., white wall, lost frames) without a broader systematic study of failure modes of the proposed method itself, beyond the brief points in the Limitations section.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated technical contribution: reformulating context conditioning for camera-controllable video generation to leverage both temporal and spatial adjacency, addressing a real limitation of prior video-to-future-video and single-frame camera-controllable methods.

Careful and non-trivial dynamic masking pipeline (optical-flow thresholding + backward point tracking with CoTracker3 + SAM2 propagation) that convincingly solves the ghosting-artifact problem of naive point-cloud aggregation, with clear qualitative evidence (Fig. 4/5).

Extensive and diverse experimental evaluation across multiple axes (spatial/geometric consistency, camera controllability, video quality) on multiple datasets (RealEstate10K, DynPose-100K, DAVIS for long video), with consistent, often large improvements over relevant baselines (e.g., 77% MEt3R error reduction over DFoT).

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each design choice: dynamic masking stages, number of spatial views n, temporal window size w, and choice of SLAM/depth backbone (MegaSAM vs DepthAnything v3), which also demonstrates the modularity and practicality of the framework (large inference-time reduction with similar/better quality).
Good positioning relative to related and concurrent work (DFoT, CameraCtrl2, Gen3C, SPMem, WorldMem), with explicit discussion of differences, strengthening the novelty claim.

Promising extension to long-video (autoregressive) generation included in the appendix, showing the spatial-memory idea generalizes beyond single-chunk generation, with honest acknowledgment of remaining drift issues.
Reasonable reproducibility: builds on open-sourced CogVideoX-I2V-5B with minimal architectural changes, detailed training/fine-tuning hyperparameters, and a promise to release code.
weaknesses: All evaluation relies on automated metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD/VBench/MEt3R); no human/user study is conducted to assess perceptual video quality, realism of dynamic motion, or scene-consistency as judged by humans, which is important for generative video work.

The method depends on a chain of off-the-shelf components (dynamic SLAM, optical flow, CoTracker3, SAM2) whose individual failure modes (e.g., on fast motion, crowded/occluded scenes, or textureless regions) are not deeply analyzed; the paper shows average metrics but limited discussion of failure cases.

Some baselines (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl) were not designed for this exact scene-consistent multi-frame-context task, making comparisons somewhat uneven even though the authors adapt them fairly; the strongest and most comparable baseline (DFoT) is evaluated on a comparatively narrower set of experiments.

Long-video (autoregressive) generation results, while promising, are preliminary and the paper explicitly notes unresolved long-term drift/error accumulation, leaving the headline 'arbitrary-length' claim only partially substantiated.

Computational overhead of the SLAM/3D-memory construction step is non-trivial in the default configuration (over 9 minutes total, dominated by MegaSAM), and while a lighter alternative is shown, scalability of the 3D memory (storage/retrieval cost) for very long videos beyond the tested datasets is not analyzed.

Ablation studies are conducted on relatively small subsets (e.g., DynPose-100K subset, DAVIS) without clear description of subset size/selection, which slightly limits confidence in the generality of the reported gains.
